execution and what's the problem it
solves. So, when we work on enterprise

problem of what we could call workflows
or long-running business transactions,

you need to do over here. Maybe I need
to send a message over to another
service. Maybe there's like a batch job
which is for instance processing your
purchase orders and you know, moves them
to their life cycle from one state to
another. So, we have these long-running
activities in our applications. That's a
very common situation. The problem is
reasoning about those processes can be
very hard if it's implemented in
different systems, different components,
different jobs. So, it's just very hard
to understand what's the end-to-end
flow. So, what happens if I receive a
purchase order in my system? What
actually happens? It gets sent over to
the shipment service and some component
is processing it over there. Maybe
something goes wrong. So, how do I have

execution is to essentially take a very

processes essentially as a plain program

Could be Java, could be anything really,

me. So, we write our program end-to-end
in plain code.
Then the special twist is that those
individual steps in that flow, they are
essentially units of persisting state

they should happen, of course, in the

want to assign stock twice to the same
purchase order if something goes wrong.
And so, the idea here is write those
things as a plain Java program, but then
have some sort of engine around it which
takes those steps and which essentially
materializes their progress. So, for

system to, I don't know, assign stock.
And then we take the result of that and
we restore it in a local state store.
And this is where SQLite comes into the

processing the shipment later on,

the idea of durable execution. Give you

>> So, Apache parquet is a widely used file
format for storing data in a columnar
way. So, if you think about maybe a CSV
files, they store data essentially in a
row-based fashion, right? So, each
record which you want to persist in your
CSV file, it's like a new line. And this
is good for some use cases, but it's not
so good for other use cases. So, think
about a situation where you for instance
want to aggregate all the values from a
given field of your data. So, let's say
you want to
aggregate the entire value of all your
purchase orders. So, with a CSV file or
row-based file like that, you would have
to kind of go through all the files,
find purchase order field and sum up
those values. So, it wouldn't be very
fast and
exactly for those kinds of use cases,
there's this idea, okay, let's store
data not row-based, but column-based.
So, all the values from one column, like
order value, we store all those
sequentially and we do that for all the
columns of our data set. And now this
has a few advantages. So, we can very
selectively query the data. So, if you
are interested in just aggregating all
the value from the purchase order value
column, we just can sequentially read
the data, all the purchase order values
of each order. So, it's very fast to
read. We don't even have to do the IO
for all the other columns because we are
not interested. So, that's very
efficient. And then also, storing the
data becomes very efficient that way
because
if you think about for instance
timestamps, maybe your data set is
ordered. So, what you could do is
instead of storing each timestamp like
as its own fully self-contained value,
you could just persist the first one and
then for the next one you just restore
the data. Maybe it's just like 2
milliseconds later, so you just store a
two instead of a full timestamp, so it's
very space-efficient. And then also
it's, you know, lends itself very well
towards compression. So, essentially
that's the reasons why those columnar

default file format, I would say, in

you know, I could, for instance, start

as much CPU as I can.

then by those primitive arrays, right?
